                                      PROJECT NO. 58481


RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §                  OF TEXAS
STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                    §




        SPLIGHT COMMENTS ON STAFF'S DRAFT DISCUSSION RULE § 25.194

        Splight Inc. (“Splight”) appreciates the work that the Public Utility Commission of Texas
(commission) and Staff are doing to implement Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §37.0561
as enacted by Senate Bill (SB) 6 in the above-referenced proceeding. The following comments are
offered in response to Staff’s recommendation proposing new 16 Texas Administrative Code
(TAC) §25.194 to implement Large Load Interconnection Standards. Our suggestions here are
aimed at strengthening the rule to help achieve the primary goal of SB 6, that is, managing the
rapidly increasing demand for power on the transmission system by large loads while supporting
the economic activity this development will bring.



   I.      ABOUT SPLIGHT

        Founded in 2021, Splight is an international provider of scalable grid technology solutions
with operations in North America, Latin America, and Europe. Splight has developed and deployed
a new digital technology to increase transmission capability while adding reliability and flexibility
to the grid. Splight’s platform uses intelligent computing and real-time controls and
communications to automatically and dynamically reduce demand or injection on the system in
order to accommodate actual system capacity in response to a system failure. Splight’s solution
can bridge the capacity demand gap until physical network upgrades are completed by utilities and
can remain in place as a visualization tool and extra protective layer, ensuring reliability of grid
systems as they continually expand and increase in complexity. To reiterate, these transmission
upgrades can and should still be made, but this technology helps maintain grid reliability in the
interim to facilitate faster, lower-cost interconnections without waiting for long-lead transmission
upgrades

                                             Page 1 of 7
    II.      RECOMMENDATION THAT RELIABILITY BENEFITS OF LOADS WITH
            BACKUP GENERATION AND ADVANCED RESPONSE CAPABILITIES
            WARRANT EXPEDITED STUDY AND ADDITIONAL CAPACITY
            ALLOCATION

         In Sections (c)(5), (e)(7) and (h)(7), the commission requires utilities to obtain detailed
information about a large load applicant’s proposed on-site generation if it meets the definition of
“backup generator.” While this disclosure is clearly necessary for the utility and ERCOT to
adequately assess the potential impacts of load interconnection, the draft rule does not currently
provide guidance or instruction on how such information should be considered within the study
process. We recommend that the commission recognize the different relationship that a load with
backup generation can have with the system compared to those without. Specifically, loads that
install responsive generation or storage for the purpose of individually responding to resource or
transmission adequacy challenges of the market or system operator should have that capability
accounted for within the interconnection study process, if the applicant load requests it. Reliability
benefits can be used as a basis for both (1) expedited interconnection study and (2) allocation of
increased capacity in consideration of the speed and amount of curtailment a load is willing and
able to provide in response to the needs of the market or transmission system. This could be a
crucial element to help support the speed to market for data centers and other organic industrial
growth in the state.

         If an applicant load will be capable of responding to resource adequacy shortages (“flexible
load”), then it should be studied as non-firm load, in accordance with its responsiveness (i.e.,
required notice period), if ERCOT can provide the notice required in a functional format. If the
load will be capable of responding to transmission system failures (“fast-responding load”), within
a time frame to make post contingency-response sufficient to protect the remaining system after
such failures (500 milliseconds or less, as defined by ERCOT), it should be studied as firm,
according to its true impact on the delivery system reliability. Naturally, if an applicant requests
such studies, there may be related increases to the study costs of the utility and ERCOT for which


                                              Page 2 of 7
 the load would need to bear responsibility. However, because flexible and fast-responding loads
can significantly reduce operational risks to the grid, expedited treatment is warranted.

        There are a few ways the commission could incorporate effectuating language within §
25.194. Using Section (c)(5) as an example, the following text could be added to incorporate the
aforementioned recommended study requirements (new language in italics):

        (5) Backup generating facilities. A large load customer must disclose to the
interconnecting electric utility whether the customer plans to have on-site backup generating
facilities. If the large load customer plans to have on-site backup generating facilities, the large
load customer must also disclose the following information:

        (A) the number of backup generating facilities;

        (B) the nameplate capacity of each of the backup generating facilities;

        (C) the fuel source and operational characteristics of each of the backup generating
facilities; and

        (D) how quickly each of the large load customer' s backup generating facilities can turn on
to begin serving the load.

        (i)       If large load and associated backup generating facilities are capable of sub-second
                  response, whether as a dynamically responsive grid reliability asset or through
                  simple disconnection in response to a set of constraining contingencies, the
                  interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT shall study and allocate the large load’s
                  transmission capacity, on a firm capacity basis, with the assumption that the fast
                  responding load will not be drawing on the system in the event of an N-1 or higher
                  level system failure. Additional capacity allocated to a specific load as a result of
                  this predicated on the incremental capability such flexibility frees up within the
                  system, up to the maximum reliable physical capacity of the system; or
        (ii)      If the large load and corresponding backup generating facilities meet the minimum
                  requirements of this rule to be required to respond or, are capable of flexibly
                  reducing or curtailing demand from the system in response to a resource adequacy
                  issue within a prescribed timeframe, as determined by ERCOT, the interconnecting


                                               Page 3 of 7
                electric utility and ERCOT shall study and allocate the large load’s transmission
               capacity, on a non-firm capacity basis .

       Splight alternatively recommends building this into Section (l), ERCOT Operational
Standards, as follows:

                         (l) ERCOT may establish operational standards for large load customers to
               ensure system reliability.

                         (2) ERCOT may establish criteria whereby a large load customer that meets
               certain reliability-enhancing operational standards, including the ability of a large
               load to, within a prescribed timeframe:

                         (A) flexibly respond during periods of resource adequacy deficiency; and/or

                         (B) rapidly curtail in the event of a transmission system contingency

               is studied by the interconnecting utility and ERCOT, if requested, on an expedited
               interconnection timeline, and for an amount of additional transmission capacity,
               which accounts for the speed of curtailment the combined load and onsite backup
               generation offer in response to the relevant most limiting transmission line rating
               in the event of a system contingency.

                         (2) A large load customer must comply with operational standards,
               developed through ERCOT protocols, as a condition for interconnection and
               continued operation of customer' s load.

                         (3) An interconnecting electric utility, including a municipal or cooperative
               utility shall cooperate with the large load, and its technology solution provider
               where appropriate, offering the technological capability to reduce or curtail demand
               in response to transmission system failures, within a time frame acceptable to
               ERCOT, by allowing access to system data required to trigger such response, or
               otherwise provide the real-time signal required for a timely response to a system
               contingency.

In sum, the interconnection rule should provide not only the recognition of the various levels of
voluntary “flexibility” presented by different loads, but also the applicant’s right to be evaluated

                                               Page 4 of 7
 by the interconnecting utility, and subsequently by ERCOT, based on the advanced capabilities of
the interconnecting applicant, and therefore its actual impact on the market or the electric delivery
system - or both. And, the interconnecting utility, and ERCOT, must allow the applicant load
seeking to be individually treated as a flexible, or fast-responding load, access to the system data
required to assure execution of such capability.



   III.         REQUEST FOR SECTION-SPECIFIC CLARIFICATIONS

          In Section (b), Definitions, paragraph (3), “Discretionary services agreement” requires
that the defined agreement meet the requirements of the following Section (d), but it would
appear that the intent is to reference Section (e). In addition, because “discretionary services” is
already a term of art in the industry, used for a broader range of additional negotiated services of
the utility for a given customer, the use of this term “discretionary” in this context may prove
confusing. Because the proposed definition would narrow the definition of a “discretionary
services agreement” to a specific case for a specific class of customer, we suggest that the
commission select a new term for this particular application

          (3)     Large Load Interconnection Annex Discretionary services agreement -- An A
          discretionary services agreement, executed and securitized by a large load customer and
          interconnecting electric utility after the interconnecting electric utility completes the large
          load interconnection study and before the interconnecting electric utility submits the
          study to ERCOT, that, at a minimum, satisfies subsection (de) of this section., and
          becomes an attachment to the final large load interconnection agreement when final.

In Section (c)(1), the “large load customer” is asked to distinguish whether the “customer” is a
developer or an “end-use customer.” We understand the intent, however, there is again a
potential for confusion in this language using customer in three contexts, particularly given the
explicit and exclusive definitions of “End-use customer” in (b)(4), “Large load customer” in
(b)(7) and “Project developer” in (b)(10). The issue arises again in Sections (e)(1), and (h)(1) as
well. We recommend alternative language such as:




                                                Page 5 of 7
        (1)     Project developer or end-use customer. A large load customer interconnection
       applicant must disclose to the interconnecting utility whether the customer applicant is a
       project developer or an end-use customer.

       Other sections also refer to the large load “customer,” and simply the “customer,”
although the apparent use of the term would reflect the commission’s intent to include either the
end-use “customer” or the “project developer,” as appropriate. Paragraph (c)(3), for example,
could be read to mean only the end-use “customer” must disclose information, when the
commission likely intended to mean the interconnection applicant, whether it is the “project
developer” or the “end-use customer.” As such, we recommend either clarifying this, or
introducing the encompassing term “applicant” or, some alternative third term. If the
commission agrees that this could help clarify the intent and applicability of the rule proposed, it
will need to make the necessary substitutions throughout the proposed rule, and may also want to
add the new term (e.g., Applicant) to the definitions, in Section (b).

       V. CONCLUSION

       Splight respectfully and sincerely hopes that the commission will maximize this
opportunity to help unlock significant transmission capacity, reduce interconnection backlogs, and
support the state’s growing demand for electricity in a secure and sustainable manner.




Dated: December 19, 2025

 SPLIGHT EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

   Although the rule provides requirements for the interconnection of large loads, it does not
appropriately recognize the potential benefits of flexibility, or fast-responding load capabilities in
the study process in such a manner that might support either the accelerated interconnection of,
or expanded capacity to be made available to, such loads. SB6 includes among its objectives,
besides the management of large load impacts and maintaining the reliability of the system, also
the state support of economic development. Therefore, we make the following recommendations.

       •   Large loads willing and able to reliably and individually respond flexibly to resource
           shortage should be studied as interruptible, or non-firm load, if requested of the
           interconnecting electric utility, including a municipal or cooperative utility.
       •   Large loads willing and able to reliably and individually respond in real-time to
           transmission system failures (within 500 milliseconds or less as required by ERCOT
           to qualify as an appropriate response to an N-1 or higher system contingency), should
           have the right to be studied as a firm load, but credited with their actual system
           impacts if they will not in fact be a factor in a relevant contingency.
       •   The interconnecting electric utility, including municipal or cooperative utility, and
           ERCOT, must cooperate with the large load, and its technology solution provider(s)
           where appropriate, to provide data, or data access, in the necessary time-frame
           associated with either system resource shortages or expected shortages, or with
           elements of the transmission system that are potentially constraining in a system
           failure of any kind.
       •   The proposed rule potentially creates some confusion of terms in adoption of two
           terms. First, Discretionary Service Agreement is already a term of use, and the
           proposed use is a subcategory of such agreements and should be treated as such. The
           use of the term “customer” alone introduces potential ambiguity, where it is meant to
           represent defined terms “end-use customer,” “large load customer,” and/or “project
           developer.”
